# Atwell Mill Campground
## Reservations
Reservations for Atwell Mill Campground typically open in April and can be made up to one month in advance of your stay. All sites are reservation only.
Image Gallery
A sign reads "Atwell Mill Campground" near a narrow road
Picnic tables on level ground in a shady forest
A primitive restroom building
A marker with an accessibility symbol near a forested campsite
The roads leading to the campground are extremely narrow and winding.
NPS Photo
Atwell Mill's campsites are in a shady sequoia grove.
NPS Photo
The ground around the restroom is level and firm-packed.
NPS Photo
This accessible campsite features level, firm-packed surfaces.
NPS Photo
Accessibility Information
ADA Information - While there are currently no accessible campsites, our parks are committed to creating sites in the near future.
Wheelchair Access - Campground roads are unpaved, rutted, and uneven.
RV & Trailer Information - No RVs or trailers permitted in campground.
RV Allowed - No
Trailer Allowed - No
Classification - This campground is a designated primitive campsite.

# Atwell Mill Campground
## Reservations
#### Other Information
You are required to store food properly in order to protect bears. Each campsite has a large food storage locker (47”W x 33”D x 28”H) that is resistant to bears when properly latched. Learn more about bears and food storage in the parks.
Protect your car from marmots. Marmots will chew through car wiring and radiator hosing, disabling the vehicle. They are especially active in Mineral King in spring and early summer. Use tarp to cover your vehicle's undercarriage and prepare with marmot safety tips.
Pets are permitted within the campground, but must be leashed at all times. Learn more about pet regulations.
An interactive map of the campground can be viewed in the reservation section above or on the Atwell Mill Campground page on recreation.gov.

Source: https://dirtygourmet.com/2014/09/02/atwell-mill-campground-mineral-king-in-sequoia-national-park/
Title: Atwell Mill Campground, Sequoia National Park – Dirty Gourmet
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6
Every year in August, Wes and I go on a backpacking trip. We wait until the very end of the summer, which helps us miss most of the crowds. This year, our trip counted as our Honeymoon. We originally talked about going somewhere far far away (Olympic, Glacier, Tetons!), but realized that would really cut into our backcountry time with all the traveling, and we wanted to get deep into the woods this time. Instead of far, we went to one of our closest national parks- Sequoia.
As usual, we went with barely a loose plan, hoping the rangers would direct us. We wanted to be out for around 5 days, and we wanted a loop. The first ranger we spoke to said he worked in Mineral King, which was up a frightening one-lane, blind-curve-filled 25 mile road that took two hours to get up. He called the road the “limiting factor” for crowds, though, so we headed straight there.
Our backpacking trip was a 60ish mile, 6 day loop over Franklin Pass, down Rattlesnake Creek, up the Kern River (hitting Kern Hot Spring while we were there), and back up over Sawtooth Pass. It included over 12,000 feet in elevation gain, and then the same amount of elevation loss. It was absolutely worth every step. The terrain changed so often that we were never bored and always in awe. We saw bears, fawns, waterfalls, alpine lakes, views of Whitney, and glorious sunsets. And the hot spring was located halfway through the trip, which was the perfect time to rest our weary muscles for the rest of the road ahead.
Of course, we gathered some new delicious recipes, but I thought I’d start with the gem of a camping location we found on our first night. Atwell Mill Campground was our staging site the night before the actual backpacking began. Though the road is rough, you pass several “monarch” sized Giant Sequoias on your way up, and actually stay among the Atwell grove. The smell of the moist air and soil surrounds you and the ground is soft for sleeping. The elevation is perfect for cool fall camping, but there’s only a little bit of time left to enjoy it before the road closes for the winter.
We love fall camping, and would love to hear where you like to go so we can check it out!

## Atwell Mill Campground, Mineral King
### Location
Mineral King, CA

## Atwell Mill Campground, Mineral King
### Activity Guide
Car Camping, Hiking, Giant tree viewing

## Atwell Mill Campground, Mineral King
### General Info
Atwell Mill Campground is the site of a sequoia grove that was milled before the big trees were protected. It is located most of the way up the long and slow Mineral King Road, at around 7000 feet of elevation. It is only open from May 21- October 15.

## Atwell Mill Campground, Mineral King
### Amenities
*   Gorgeous scenery  
*   Bear lockers  
*   Tent campsites only  
*   Pit toilets

## Atwell Mill Campground, Mineral King
### Insider Information
1.   This campground is closer and less populated than Cold Spring Campground, which is closer to the ranger station in Silver City Resort 5 miles up the road.  
2.   Hikes out of this area are all phenomenal, and if you’re willing to do a strenuous hike, you can up get to several lakes, including Monarch, Crystal, Franklin, and Columbine.  
3.   Franklin Pass is easier to get over than Sawtooth going this direction, and you’ll have to go over Sawtooth Pass to get to Columbine Lake.  
4.   The wildlife in this area is prevalent and fun to see, but obviously desensitized to human interaction. Please be mindful of food at all times and keep wildlife wild.

**Atwell Mill Grove** is a special place in California. It is home to many giant sequoia trees. These are some of the biggest trees on Earth! The grove is found in the Kaweah River area. It is part of the famous Sequoia National Park.
You can reach Atwell Mill Grove by driving on Mineral King Road. This road branches off from California State Route 198. It is located near the south entrance to Sequoia National Park.

## Contents
### Where is Atwell Mill Grove?
The grove is about 1.5 miles (2.4 km) west of a small community. This community is called Silver City. It is also about 19 miles (30.6 km) from Highway 198. The road leading into this part of the park is narrow. It can be a bit tricky to drive on.

## Contents
### What is Atwell Mill Campground?
Inside the grove, you will find the Atwell Mill Campground. It is located on the East Fork of the Kaweah River. This part of the grove was once used for logging. Logging means cutting down trees for wood. The trees here were cut before they were fully protected.
Atwell Mill was once a lumber mill. A lumber mill is a factory where logs are processed. They are turned into useful wood products. This mill used to process logs from the Atwell Mill Grove.

## Amazing Giant Sequoias
Atwell Mill Grove has some truly amazing giant sequoia trees. These trees are very old and very large. Here are a few of the most famous ones:

## Amazing Giant Sequoias
### The Diamond Tree
The Diamond Tree grows on a very steep slope. It is taller than most trees in the grove. It stands at almost 290 feet (88 meters) tall. This makes it the largest tree in the entire grove.

## Amazing Giant Sequoias
### The Above Diamond Tree
Just above the Diamond Tree, you will find the Above Diamond Tree. This is why it is called the "AD Tree." Its main trunk is very thick and strong.

## Amazing Giant Sequoias
### The Dean Tree
The Dean Tree is incredibly large. It has a volume of 32,333 cubic feet (915 cubic meters). This huge size places it among the top 30 giant sequoias in the world!

## Amazing Giant Sequoias
### The Arm Tree
The Arm Tree is also known as the "Big Limb Tree." It has the largest known limb of any tree in the world. This massive limb is about 12 feet (3.7 meters) across!

You are required to store food properly in order to protect bears. Each campsite has a large food storage locker (47”W x 33”D x 28”H) that is resistant to bears when properly latched. Learn more about bears and food storage in the parks.

Pets are permitted within the campground, but must be leashed at all times. Learn more about pet regulations.

Every year in August, Wes and I go on a backpacking trip. We wait until the very end of the summer, which helps us miss most of the crowds. This year, our trip counted as our Honeymoon. We originally talked about going somewhere far far away (Olympic, Glacier, Tetons!), but realized that would really cut into our backcountry time with all the traveling, and we wanted to get deep into the woods this time. Instead of far, we went to one of our closest national parks- Sequoia.
As usual, we went with barely a loose plan, hoping the rangers would direct us. We wanted to be out for around 5 days, and we wanted a loop. The first ranger we spoke to said he worked in Mineral King, which was up a frightening one-lane, blind-curve-filled 25 mile road that took two hours to get up. He called the road the “limiting factor” for crowds, though, so we headed straight there.
Our backpacking trip was a 60ish mile, 6 day loop over Franklin Pass, down Rattlesnake Creek, up the Kern River (hitting Kern Hot Spring while we were there), and back up over Sawtooth Pass. It included over 12,000 feet in elevation gain, and then the same amount of elevation loss. It was absolutely worth every step. The terrain changed so often that we were never bored and always in awe. We saw bears, fawns, waterfalls, alpine lakes, views of Whitney, and glorious sunsets. And the hot spring was located halfway through the trip, which was the perfect time to rest our weary muscles for the rest of the road ahead.
Of course, we gathered some new delicious recipes, but I thought I’d start with the gem of a camping location we found on our first night. Atwell Mill Campground was our staging site the night before the actual backpacking began. Though the road is rough, you pass several “monarch” sized Giant Sequoias on your way up, and actually stay among the Atwell grove. The smell of the moist air and soil surrounds you and the ground is soft for sleeping. The elevation is perfect for cool fall camping, but there’s only a little bit of time left to enjoy it before the road closes for the winter.
We love fall camping, and would love to hear where you like to go so we can check it out!

## Atwell Mill Campground, Mineral King
### General Info
Atwell Mill Campground is the site of a sequoia grove that was milled before the big trees were protected. It is located most of the way up the long and slow Mineral King Road, at around 7000 feet of elevation. It is only open from May 21- October 15.

## Atwell Mill Campground, Mineral King
### Amenities
*   Gorgeous scenery  
*   Bear lockers  
*   Tent campsites only  
*   Pit toilets

## Atwell Mill Campground, Mineral King
### Insider Information
1.   This campground is closer and less populated than Cold Spring Campground, which is closer to the ranger station in Silver City Resort 5 miles up the road.  
2.   Hikes out of this area are all phenomenal, and if you’re willing to do a strenuous hike, you can up get to several lakes, including Monarch, Crystal, Franklin, and Columbine.  
3.   Franklin Pass is easier to get over than Sawtooth going this direction, and you’ll have to go over Sawtooth Pass to get to Columbine Lake.  
4.   The wildlife in this area is prevalent and fun to see, but obviously desensitized to human interaction. Please be mindful of food at all times and keep wildlife wild.

**Atwell Mill Grove** is a special place in California. It is home to many giant sequoia trees. These are some of the biggest trees on Earth! The grove is found in the Kaweah River area. It is part of the famous Sequoia National Park.
You can reach Atwell Mill Grove by driving on Mineral King Road. This road branches off from California State Route 198. It is located near the south entrance to Sequoia National Park.

## Contents
### Where is Atwell Mill Grove?
The grove is about 1.5 miles (2.4 km) west of a small community. This community is called Silver City. It is also about 19 miles (30.6 km) from Highway 198. The road leading into this part of the park is narrow. It can be a bit tricky to drive on.

## Contents
### What is Atwell Mill Campground?
Inside the grove, you will find the Atwell Mill Campground. It is located on the East Fork of the Kaweah River. This part of the grove was once used for logging. Logging means cutting down trees for wood. The trees here were cut before they were fully protected.
Atwell Mill was once a lumber mill. A lumber mill is a factory where logs are processed. They are turned into useful wood products. This mill used to process logs from the Atwell Mill Grove.

## Amazing Giant Sequoias
Atwell Mill Grove has some truly amazing giant sequoia trees. These trees are very old and very large. Here are a few of the most famous ones:

## Amazing Giant Sequoias
### The Diamond Tree
The Diamond Tree grows on a very steep slope. It is taller than most trees in the grove. It stands at almost 290 feet (88 meters) tall. This makes it the largest tree in the entire grove.

## Amazing Giant Sequoias
### The Above Diamond Tree
Just above the Diamond Tree, you will find the Above Diamond Tree. This is why it is called the "AD Tree." Its main trunk is very thick and strong.

## Amazing Giant Sequoias
### The Dean Tree
The Dean Tree is incredibly large. It has a volume of 32,333 cubic feet (915 cubic meters). This huge size places it among the top 30 giant sequoias in the world!

## Amazing Giant Sequoias
### The Arm Tree
The Arm Tree is also known as the "Big Limb Tree." It has the largest known limb of any tree in the world. This massive limb is about 12 feet (3.7 meters) across!
